hints: Think about which hydride reducing agent is strong enough to reduce a carboxylic acid all the way to a primary alcohol, NaBH4 is too weak for this.
walkthrough:
Recall the two hydride reducers**
You have two to choose from at AS level. $\text{NaBH}_{4}$ reduces only aldehydes and ketones. Carboxylic acids are much harder to reduce, so you need the stronger powerhouse, lithium aluminium hydride.
Final answer: $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$

hints: Count oxygen atoms on each side, propanoic acid has two O atoms but propan-1-ol has only one, so water must be the second product to balance O.
walkthrough:
Balance using [H] as your tool**
Think of $[\text{H}]$ as hydrogen atoms supplied by $\text{Q}$. Start with $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COOH}$. To become $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ you need to remove one O as $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ and add hydrogens. Balancing atoms gives: $$\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CO}_{2}\text{H} + 4[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ Check: 6 H on left from $4[\text{H}]$ plus 6 in acid equals 8 in alcohol plus 2 in water, and 2 O each side.

hints: Focus on what happens to the OH group when SOCl2 reacts with propan-1-ol, which atom replaces it to form compound E.
walkthrough:
Spot the swap**
Propan-1-ol $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ plus $\text{SOCl}_{2}$ gives $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$ (compound E). The $\text{OH}$ group is directly swapped for $\text{Cl}$. When one group replaces another in this way, that is substitution.

hints: Compare carbon counts, E is a 3-carbon chloroalkane but butanenitrile has 4 carbons, so think which nucleophile adds one carbon.
walkthrough:
Choose the carbon adding reagent**
You need to turn $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Cl}$ into $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CN}$. The $\text{CN}^{-}$ ion is the nucleophile that replaces $\text{Cl}$ and adds the extra carbon. Use potassium cyanide dissolved in ethanol with heating, ethanol is used because the chloroalkane does not dissolve in water and aqueous conditions would give the alcohol.
Final answer: $\text{KCN}$ in ethanol / $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH}$ AND heat

hints: Recall that heating a nitrile with NaOH(aq) does not give the free acid, it gives the sodium carboxylate salt plus ammonia.
Write the nitrile as $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CN}$ and balance Na, N, O and H with NaOH and H2O on the left.
walkthrough:
Identify the organic product**
Under alkaline conditions the $\text{CN}$ carbon becomes $\text{CO}_{2}^{-}$. So butanenitrile $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CN}$ becomes sodium butanoate $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CO}_{2}\text{Na}$, and nitrogen leaves as $\text{NH}_{3}$.

Complete the balanced equation**
Add $\text{NaOH}$ and $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ to supply O, Na and H: $$\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CN} + \text{NaOH} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CO}_{2}\text{Na} + \text{NH}_{3}$$ This balances all atoms and gives compound T as the butanoate salt.

hints: Think of the general name for breaking the C triple bond N in a nitrile with water in alkaline solution.
walkthrough:
Name the water splitting process**
Water is adding across the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ bond to make $\text{CO}_{2}^{-}$ and $\text{NH}_{3}$. Any reaction where water breaks bonds in a molecule is hydrolysis, here it is alkaline hydrolysis because $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ is used.
Final answer: (alkaline) hydrolysis

hints: Recall the geometry and hybridisation of a carbon with four single sigma bonds and no pi bonds.
walkthrough:
Link saturated to hybridisation**
Saturated means each carbon has four single bonds, tetrahedral arrangement, bond angle about $109.5^{\circ}$. That always comes from $\text{sp}^{3}$ hybridisation of carbon.

hints: Recall the general equation, 2ROH + 2Na gives 2RONa plus which gas that pops with a lit splint.
walkthrough:
Remember the classic observation**
Sodium fizzes in any alcohol to give the alkoxide and a colourless gas: $$2\text{ROH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{RONa} + \text{H}_{2}$$ That gas is hydrogen, $\text{H}_{2}$.
Final answer: hydrogen / $\text{H}_{2}$

hints: Track oxidation number, Na changes from 0 in Na(s) to +1 in RONa, so has it lost or gained electrons and what does that make it.
walkthrough:
Apply OILRIG to sodium**
$\text{Na}$ goes from $0$ to $+1$, it loses electrons, it is oxidised. A species that loses electrons while causing the other reactant to gain electrons is a reducing agent. So $\text{Na}$ reduces the alcohol by donating electrons to it.
Final answer: (It / Na) reduces A / B / C / the alcohol (group) OR (it / Na behaves as) reducing agent OR (it / Na) donates electrons to A / B / C / the alcohol (group)

hints: Use the dichromate result first, A remains orange so it is not oxidised, which class of alcohol resists oxidation by acidified K2Cr2O7.
walkthrough:
Decode A from both tests**
Heat with acidified $\text{K}_{2}\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$ stays orange means no oxidation, so A must be tertiary. With four carbons there is only one tertiary alcohol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol: $$(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{COH}$$ Its lack of reaction with alkaline $\text{I}_{2}$ (no visible change) fits, as it has no $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)}$ group.

hints: B turns dichromate green so it is primary or secondary, but gives no yellow precipitate with alkaline I2, so it lacks the CH3CH(OH) group.
walkthrough:
Narrow down B**
Orange to green means B is oxidised, so primary or secondary. No pale yellow precipitate with alkaline $\text{I}_{2}$ means no $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)}$ group and not ethanal-like structure. The remaining four-carbon primary alcohols without that group are $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$, butan-1-ol, and $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{OH}$, 2-methylpropan-1-ol.
Final answer: butan-1-ol OR (2) methylpropan-1-ol

hints: C is oxidised by dichromate and gives a positive iodoform test, so look for the four-carbon alcohol containing a CH3CH(OH) group.
walkthrough:
Pinpoint C**
Orange to green shows C is primary or secondary. Pale yellow precipitate with warm alkaline $\text{I}_{2}$ is the triiodomethane test for $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)}$. The only four-carbon alcohol that fits both is butan-2-ol: $$\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{3}$$ It is oxidised to butanone which then gives $\text{CHI}_{3}$.
Final answer: butan-2-ol OR $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_{3}$
